title: The Borrowed Radiators
premise: After her father's funeral, Wren Eastwick inventories his house and his silences, cataloging everything he never told her. Then a late-night radio station broadcasts a song she recognizes as one her father wrote and never recorded — sung by a stranger, credited to a name she's never heard. Chasing the broadcast, Wren uncovers a decades-old promise between two friends, an unfinished debt of authorship, and a sentence her father left untranslated in a language only one other living person can read. To claim her inheritance, she must give it away: the song, the credit, and the truth, before the station's final broadcast and the last person who remembers goes silent forever.
about_author: Vesper Ishikawa is a former radio archivist who spent six years cataloging orphaned recordings before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, silence, and the strange justice of things returned too late.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, catalogs her father's house after the funeral: unlabeled keys, a locked drawer, a notebook of half-sentences. She inventories what he never said as if grief were an accounting problem. The emotional beat is controlled numbness cracking at the edges when she finds a lyric sheet with no melody attached.

chapters.title: The Frequency at 2 A.M.
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Unable to sleep, she scans the radio dial and hears a song she has never heard but somehow knows — her father's unrecorded lyric, set to music, sung by a voice that isn't his. The DJ credits it to 'T. Okafor.' The beat is vertigo: the dead speaking in a language she thought was private.

chapters.title: What the Will Doesn't Cover
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, interviews the executor and an aunt, learning her father once played music with someone named Tomas. Everyone remembers the friendship, no one remembers the ending. The beat is the first fracture in her image of her father: he had a whole life she was never told about.

chapters.title: A Stranger's Voice
chapters.summary: Wren traces the broadcast to a community station and meets Marisol, the DJ, who plays 'orphaned songs' — works whose owners never claimed them. She has a tape, mailed anonymously, postmarked the week before Wren's father died. The beat is cautious alliance; two keepers of other people's unfinished business.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, finds in the locked drawer a letter to Tomas written in their childhood private language — a code only the two of them could read. One sentence remains undeciphered, circled twice. The beat is obsession taking hold: she cannot inherit what she cannot read.

chapters.title: Tomas Okafor, Deceased, Allegedly
chapters.summary: Wren discovers Tomas officially died thirty years ago — yet someone is alive who codes like him. She visits the last address, finds a boarded house and a neighbor who says 'he comes back every spring.' The beat is uncanny dread braided with hope.

chapters.title: The Second Listener
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV. She reveals the anonymous mailer has sent tapes for years, always timed to anniversaries she doesn't understand. She plays Wren the earliest one: two young voices, laughing, her father's. The beat is tenderness and guilt — Marisol has been keeping someone's promise without knowing for whom.

chapters.title: Everything the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, tears up floorboards of memory: a photograph of two boys under a borrowed radiator, a pawn ticket, a receipt for a bus ticket never used. The boys were inseparable until one was taken in and one was not. The beat is the slow assembly of a betrayal neither boy chose.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Radiators
chapters.summary: Wren learns the title's origin: her grandparents' house had radiators lent by the Okafors during a hard winter, never returned, a debt her father carried like a stone. The song was written to repay it. The beat is the theme crystallizing — justice outside the law, debts of warmth.

chapters.title: Someone Is Following the Same Song
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, notices a man at the station, then outside her father's house. He leaves a note: 'Stop looking. He wanted it buried.' The beat is threat — the silence her father kept had guardians, and they are still on duty.

chapters.title: The Estate of Silence
chapters.summary: The man, Ambrose, POV. He was the father's lawyer and confessor, holder of a sealed instruction: the song must never be credited, the sentence never translated, or someone loses everything. His beat is conflicted duty; he believes he is protecting Wren by erasing her.

chapters.title: Spring, Every Year
chapters.summary: Wren stakes out the boarded house and sees an old man tend a garden that isn't his. Tomas Okafor, alive, unregistered, living outside the law for thirty years because a death certificate was the only shelter he was ever offered. The beat is awe and grief: her father's silence was a hiding place.

chapters.title: Two Boys, One Winter
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV, tells the story: the radiators, the song they wrote together, the night police came for his family, and the false death record her father arranged to save him — at the cost of never speaking to him again. The beat is devastating tenderness; the silence was love in its only available form.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Wren brings the letter; Tomas reads the untranslatable sentence: an apology and an invitation — 'come home, the debt is yours to forgive, not mine to pay.' Her father died before Tomas could answer. The beat is the emotional summit of the mystery: the inheritance is a question awaiting a reply.

chapters.title: What Ambrose Is Protecting
chapters.summary: Wren confronts Ambrose and learns the sealed instruction's stakes: the false death record, if surfaced, exposes an official who falsified it — now a judge — and Tomas could lose his fragile legal existence. The beat is moral vertigo: truth and justice point in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV: the station is losing its license; the final broadcast is in nine days, and the orphaned songs will be sealed or destroyed. Wren realizes the song's only home is about to vanish. The beat is the clock starting in earnest — time is running out on every front at once.

chapters.title: A Debt Repaid in the Wrong Currency
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, tries to negotiate with the judge's office through Ambrose and fails; the system offers silence in exchange for silence. She understands the law cannot return what it took. The beat is the dark night — every legal door closes, and the radio goes quiet mid-song.

chapters.title: The Choice of the Heir
chapters.summary: Wren decides: the song will be broadcast with both names, the sentence translated, the record told — and she will take the consequences, including possible exposure of Tomas. Tomas, hearing her plan, refuses to let her pay his debts. The beat is collision of two justices: protection versus truth.

chapters.title: What the Dead Man Signs
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV, makes his own choice: he will sign an affidavit confessing his false death himself, on air, reclaiming his name before anyone can take it from him. The beat is agency reclaimed — the man who was hidden chooses to be seen, on his own terms, at his own risk.

chapters.title: Final Frequency
chapters.summary: Climax. The station's last broadcast: Marisol plays the song, Wren reads the translated sentence, Tomas speaks his name and his confession live. Ambrose arrives not to stop them but to witness; the judge's office listens, and does not intervene — or cannot. The beat is catharsis at the edge of ruin.

chapters.title: Probate of the Heart
chapters.summary: Aftermath, Wren, POV: the fallout is quieter than feared — an inquiry, a pardon in process, a judge's quiet resignation. The song is re-registered to both names. Wren closes her inventory of unsaid things and writes a new list: things said, finally, too late and exactly on time. The beat is earned peace.

chapters.title: The Returned Radiators
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Wren and Tomas, shared POV. Spring: Tomas moves into the repaired house next to the garden; Wren installs new radiators in her father's old rooms and gives the old ones, finally, to the Okafors' memory. On the radio, a new song — credited to two names, and a third: hers. The beat is belonging, inherited at last.
